body:
## Goal

Make LiteDB's existing safety guidance executable and repeatable: a locally correct PR must not silently invalidate previously supported storage, recovery, concurrency, compatibility, query, or API behavior.

The central question remains:

> **Which previously valid states, transitions, callers, and files can this change invalidate—and what evidence would detect that?**

The strategy is not simply a longer checklist or more fuzzing. It is:

**short PR declaration → affected contracts → discriminating tests → current integrated-tree evidence → bounded merge/release decision.**

This issue establishes that process and its first working examples. It does not require completing every possible audit or replacing the current test infrastructure before it can close.

`docs/rules/*` remain the normative engineering guidance; #2988 remains the storage planning epic and #2623 the authoritative release-readiness tracker. Linking a roadmap or experiment here does not automatically make all of it a v6 blocker. Concrete newly confirmed release defects receive their own issues and release dispositions.

---

## Existing building blocks: extend, do not duplicate

Baseline inspected for this refinement: `dev` at `d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3` (2026-09-28). This is an inventory, **not a claim that all listed coverage currently passes or is sufficient**.

- [Data safety](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/docs/rules/data-safety.md), [validation](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/docs/rules/validation.md), and [compatibility](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/docs/rules/compatibility.md) already require risk-scaled evidence, independent oracles, forced interleavings, and repeated recovery testing.
- [LiteDB.Fuzz](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/LiteDB.Fuzz/README.md) already provides model-based targets, raw-file integrity checks, oracle self-tests, recorded input/replay, regression corpora, and bounded campaigns. [REVIEW-AUDIT.md](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/LiteDB.Fuzz/REVIEW-AUDIT.md) already maps review findings to executable evidence.
- [Reusable CI](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/.github/workflows/_reusable-ci.yml) already runs real-version compatibility scripts and separates production builds used by tools from hook-enabled test assemblies. [Full CI](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/.github/workflows/full-ci.yml) already has a scheduled full matrix and failure reporting.

The missing connection is a maintained answer to: **which contract is covered, under which assumptions, by which scenario, on which actual revision?** Reuse these runners, manifests, reports and workflows before introducing another framework.

---

# 1. Keep the mandatory PR section small

Use five short prompts; link to deeper requirements rather than copying this whole issue into each PR:

```markdown
## Safety / regression evidence
- Contracts and risk: what stays supported, what intentionally changes, and why?
- Prior states and interactions: which existing files, callers, modes, and neighboring mechanisms are affected?
- Failure outcomes: which transitions change, and what must happen on failure, retry, disposal, or reopen?
- Evidence: tests/oracles, proof the risky path ran, failing-before evidence where applicable, and tested revision/run.
- Coverage delta and residual concerns: tests removed/weakened/replaced, remaining gaps, and the strongest plausible counterexample.
```

A documentation-only PR can give a brief justified non-applicability statement. A test-only PR changing a durability oracle, test selection, timeouts, skips, or corpus expectations is **not automatically low risk**.

Evidence scales with affected behavior, including indirect callers—not just the changed directory or lines of code. Use the existing levels in `docs/rules/validation.md`:

| Affected surface | Additional review focus |
| --- | --- |
| Local behavior | Boundary/error cases and affected callers |
| Shared query/mapper/serializer/index behavior | Independent expected semantics, cross-path comparisons, historical representations and public API behavior |
| Stateful/concurrent/ownership behavior | Forced interleavings, snapshots, progress, cleanup, repeated execution and process boundaries |
| Files/WAL/streams/sidecars | Failed and partial I/O, byte preservation, ownership, restart, exact committed contents and diagnostics |
| Upgrade/checkpoint/replacement/recovery protocols | Explicit state model, durable ordering, interruption of recovery itself, compatibility and allowed terminal states |

Path-based classification may suggest obligations, but must not silently downgrade a transitive storage/concurrency change. A changed risk classification must refresh the applicable evidence.

## Account for old tests, not merely old test names

When removing, replacing, skipping, narrowing, repinning, or weakening coverage, identify the previous invariant and where it remains covered. Include CI filters/partitions, fixture generators, expected-error allowlists, timeouts and corpus hashes in this review.

A replacement may be stronger; old code need not remain forever. But a new test proving one property does not justify losing a separate property such as sustained-contention progress. Preserve both where necessary. Intentional behavior changes need an explicit compatibility decision, not an updated golden file alone.

---

# 2. Connect contracts to executable evidence

Maintain a small index of important invariants, using stable IDs or stable documentation anchors. Do not create a second competing specification or a hand-maintained list of every test.

Start with a few high-value families:

| Contract family | Typical executable evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Acknowledged durable transactions survive within the stated fault model | Independent operation/acknowledgment history, crash/persistence faults, exact cold-reopen state |
| Recovery never combines incompatible data/WAL generations | Install/rollback transition matrix, namespace/persistence faults, old/new/refused outcome checks |
| Readers retain their admitted snapshot across writes and reclamation | Multiple observed live generations, forced overlapping writes/checkpoints/reuse, full snapshot contents |
| Supported historical inputs preserve their documented behavior | Actual producer binaries/files, explicit read/migrate/reject outcomes, indexes and mutation lifecycle |
| Query and mapping paths preserve meaning | Independent model plus applicable indexed/unindexed, cached/uncached, generated/reflection or API/SQL comparisons |

For each **identified risk in a PR**, link a compact evidence row containing:

- contract/assumptions and relevant state transition;
- test/scenario and independent expected outcome;
- observed marker, counter, plan or fault boundary proving execution;
- command/run, actual source tree, test/harness revision, runtime/architecture and relevant storage configuration;
- result and any explicit gap or limitation.

Generate repetitive metadata from CI. Authors should link evidence, not manually paste pages of logs.

Record whether a test fails on the relevant broken revision. Where the current baseline no longer reproduces, name the versions and conditions attempted; do not manufacture a failing-before claim. A deliberately broken implementation variant can validate a guard, but is not proof that a reported historical regression occurred.

**A broad green suite, a test count, or line coverage alone is not this evidence.** Coverage must include the required semantic events: e.g. a real handoff, two live snapshots, an actual retired-slot reuse, an indexed plan, or the selected crash boundary.

---

# 3. Make the safety contract precise before adding tests

## Model the lifecycle and simplify the protocol

For significant stateful changes, write down:

```
preconditions → admitted state → visible state → durable publication
             → failure/rollback → recovery/retry → cleanup
```

Describe the allowed outcomes at the affected boundaries. Include states created by a prior version and combinations produced by other recently merged features.

Review design alternatives before accumulating compensation branches: can a state be removed, publication delayed, recovery metadata retained longer, or a known-correct path kept while an optimization is isolated? A smaller protocol that can be checked convincingly is preferable to a larger protocol justified by increasingly elaborate local tests.

Small executable state-machine models are useful for difficult protocols, but introducing a formal-methods tool or rewriting the engine is not a prerequisite for this issue.

## Distinguish failure models

Do not use the word “crash-safe” without identifying what was tested:

| Model | What the evidence must distinguish |
| --- | --- |
| Exception / failed API or I/O operation | Whether cleanup/unwinding ran; transient failure versus continued failure during rollback/recovery |
| Abrupt process or owner death | No graceful engine disposal; surviving processes/OS cache/locks and cold process re-entry |
| Modeled OS/power loss | Volatile versus durable state, lost/reordered/torn writes, file creation/rename/delete and directory-entry persistence where relevant |
| OS/VM reset or physical-device campaign | Actual tested platform/storage guarantees and limitations; not inferred from a process-kill test |
| Corrupt or unsupported input | Detection/diagnostics, no silent empty/stale result, source preservation and controlled recovery/salvage contract |

A matrix covering every **registered hook** can still omit a real persistent transition. Independently review the actual I/O/ownership/publication sequence against the fault model. New hooks must enter the matrix, but missing hooks must also be discoverable.

Concrete example: #2978 is a strong install/rollback state-machine test pattern; #3011 separately tracks rebuild marker/rename directory-durability concerns. The former is not automatically evidence for the latter. Do not infer any platform's power-loss guarantee merely from “the filesystem is journaled.”

## Define transaction outcomes, not just “data must remain”

The oracle must account for full operations and transaction boundaries, including updates, deletes, uniqueness and FileStorage changes—not just retained insert IDs.

- **Durably acknowledged:** the recovered history must preserve the transaction's committed effect, subject to legitimate later transactions and the documented durability assumptions.
- **Known aborted before commit:** no partial transaction effects may leak.
- **Outcome unknown at interruption:** the transaction may have committed before its response was observed. Allow only complete outcomes permitted by the protocol; do not assume “no observed acknowledgment” means “must be absent.”
- **Explicitly degraded durability:** test the actual documented guarantee and diagnostics. Do not silently grant power-loss durability or treat a genuine I/O error as “sync unsupported.”

Keep the expected operation/acknowledgment history outside the engine under test and outside the failure domain being destroyed. A separate parent is sufficient only for a child-process failure model, not automatically for a whole-machine reset. Verify that the acknowledgment recorder itself cannot lose or misclassify completed operations.

For concurrent histories, model allowed ordering and snapshot semantics; do not impose one arbitrary schedule that the public contract never promised.

## “Fails closed” is conditional, not a universal pass

For each input/fault scenario, say which outcomes are permitted. Rejecting every valid database is not a safety fix. A valid supported file must still open, migrate or request an explicitly required writable upgrade according to its contract.

A recovery-incomplete refusal is acceptable only where that protocol permits it, with preserved evidence and actionable recovery instructions. Where automatic recovery is promised, permanent refusal after a recoverable interruption is a failure. Silent stale data is never an acceptable substitute.

Keep ordinary open/inspection, recovery and potentially lossy salvage distinct. Do not let an automatic repair hide the first failing state in a test.

---

# 4. Test composition, not only individual features

Build a small reusable set of **database lifecycle scenarios** on top of the existing targets. Reuse operation generation, fault hooks, models and artifact retention; avoid another giant bespoke harness.

Example scenario, instantiated only for supported combinations:

```
actual historical file
→ supported upgrade and legacy/new representations
→ indexed updates / transactional FileStorage changes
→ multiple live reader generations
→ another writer commits; checkpoint/reclamation is actually exercised
→ interruption at a selected boundary
→ a second interruption during recovery
→ cold open in a fresh process
→ verify complete logical state, index results and applicable structural integrity
→ further write, checkpoint and cold reopen
```

Different variants cover rebuild/replacement, Shared mapped-read admission/fallback, and query/mapper/cache interactions. Direct/Shared or mixed-version combinations that are unsupported must exercise their rejection contract, not be silently treated as supported workloads.

Select interactions by shared state, not a blind Cartesian product. Start with known dangerous pairs; add explicit multi-feature sequences where a protocol spans more than two mechanisms. Pairwise configuration coverage alone is not evidence for an ordered recovery protocol.

Exercise more than the first successful cycle: repeated recovery, cache invalidation, version resets, slot reuse, close/reopen and owner turnover. Assert that these transitions actually happened; running a loop repeatedly is not proof of them.

## Independent and complementary oracles

Use the existing logical-model, raw-integrity and differential machinery together where applicable:

- exact typed payloads, multiplicity, index keys/results, uniqueness, transaction effects and FileStorage bytes/metadata;
- raw structure/ownership/link validation, without silently rebuilding first;
- warm observations **and** fresh-process cold reads, followed by subsequent valid operations;
- indexed/unindexed or optimized/reference-path comparisons with proof each path ran.

Two paths sharing the same buggy decoder/comparer/translator are not independent. Historical versions are useful compatibility references but not universal truth for semantics intentionally changed or previously buggy. Explicitly classify expected differences.

Retain and extend `oracle-selftest`. For high-risk changes, also check that an unsafe implementation variant is detected by the **end-to-end scenario**, not only that a standalone assertion rejects a fabricated bad result. Examples: omit a durability barrier in the model, lose one acknowledged update, permit stale cleanup, bypass a generation check, or silently disable the required optimized path.

Keep instrumented deterministic tests, but also retain/extend applicable black-box production-assembly tests with `TestingEnabled=false`. Observers/barriers must not be the only reason the shipped code behaves correctly. Preserve existing production compatibility-tool coverage rather than claiming it does not exist.

## Include resource and progress contracts

Concurrency and lifetime changes must distinguish correctness, liveness and performance. Cover per-worker completed progress, bounded waits under stated scheduling assumptions, stale-handle/buffer reuse, shutdown/disposal, lease cleanup, disk/temp-space and handle/thread growth where affected.

Use timeouts as deadlock guards, not as the sole proof of the interleaving. Keep throughput/tail-latency measurements separate from deterministic correctness assertions; do not fix a liveness test by removing the competing workload.

---

# 5. Make historical compatibility a versioned contract

Extend the existing fixture corpus and real-version scripts rather than proposing a new corpus from zero.

Define expected behavior for each selected producer/consumer/configuration boundary:

| Outcome | Required assertion |
| --- | --- |
| Read directly | Exact logical/index results; promised read-only byte preservation |
| Migrate automatically | Complete safe migration, retries/interruption behavior, subsequent writes/reopen |
| Require explicit/writable upgrade | Specific actionable rejection and preserved source bytes before upgrade |
| Unsupported or older-reader rejection | No accidental fallback to legacy decoding, no truncation or other unintended mutation |

Compatibility is not “all versions can always write each other's files.” Separate released versions from intentionally supported prerelease/internal format boundaries. Include mixed-process engine versions and coordination-sidecar ABI compatibility only where support is claimed; otherwise test safe refusal/fallback.

Because prerelease packages may themselves have been publicly distributed, treat **published prereleases as an explicit policy decision rather than accidental internal-only states**. Define which published prerelease window/boundaries are covered. For those in scope, the current engine must have a declared outcome—read, migrate, explicit upgrade, or reject without mutation. Do not infer indefinite support for every historical prerelease merely because a package was once published.

Each fixture manifest should capture:

```
producer package/version or exact commit + binary hash
generator source/recipe and fixture hashes
OS/runtime/architecture/culture/collation when representation depends on them
configuration and complete data/WAL/required-sidecar bundle
independent expected logical model and index/query expectations
expected consumer read/migrate/reject behavior
provenance and reason this boundary is retained
```

Preserve originals; run mutating tests on copies. Verify both the data and relevant companions on byte-preservation/rejection paths. A changed golden fixture or logical expectation requires an explicit reviewed explanation; never regenerate it automatically from the current engine to make CI green.

Include ordinary clean/dirty WAL, plain/encrypted, indexed/unindexed, partial migration, and important mixed representations. Where relevant cover FileStorage, multikey/computed indexes, custom collation, cross-runtime ordering, finite `LIMIT_SIZE`, custom streams and capacity failure.

Start with high-value supported boundaries and expand on findings. Do not require every historical build or every configuration combination. Keep reproducible small fixtures/corpora in the repository where practical; retain larger evidence in the existing artifact repository with immutable references and sufficient retention.

A source-code revert is not necessarily a database downgrade. Record the one-way-format/recovery/backup consequences of reverting a storage change or rolling back a release.

---

# 6. Test the candidate that will actually be integrated

A PR's old green result does not validate its combination with later merges. Existing PR merge-ref checks are useful; the requirement is **fresh evidence for the actual candidate tree**, not a claim that current CI only tests isolated heads.

For affected safety-critical paths:

1. Validate against current `dev` and any preceding stack/queue changes; record the actual checkout SHA/tree and relevant dependency/tool inputs.
2. Invalidate affected evidence after a relevant head/base/stack change. An unchanged source tree may justify reusing evidence only when the relevant build inputs/configuration are also unchanged and that equivalence is recorded.
3. Use a merge queue where appropriate, or serialize high-risk merges with update/rebase and revalidation. GitHub Actions merge queues require a `merge_group` trigger; the inspected `ci.yml` does not currently have one. Verify actual repository rules and every required workflow before enabling a queue.
4. Run integrated checks after merge as a backstop and retain the last successfully validated integrated revision separately from the latest branch revision.

## Make missing evidence visible

Add a stable aggregate safety/evidence check using the existing workflows. It should verify applicability, expected jobs/tests/semantic events, tested revision, and result completeness—not pretend to evaluate the truth of prose automatically.

Required coverage must not become green through zero discovered tests, accidental filters, missing result files, a skipped selected job, an unexecuted crash hook, a timed-out worker, or a stale artifact. Intended non-applicability must be explicit. Preserve existing partition/runtime/hook verification.

Review metadata-only triggers and cancellation behavior so that label/body events cannot overwrite or cancel stronger in-progress validation with an irrelevant successful check. Keep original failed attempts and their classification; a later green rerun does not explain them.

Treat PR metadata/code as untrusted in CI; evidence collection must not require executing fork code with privileged credentials.

## Fit the cost to the stage

| Stage | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Ordinary PR | Existing baseline tests plus risk-selected regressions, mandatory sentinel/corpus cases and bounded smoke |
| High-risk merge candidate | Affected lifecycle/compatibility/interleaving/failure cases on the actual integrated tree |
| Scheduled integrated runs | Existing wider platform and fuzz campaigns, rotating seeds/combinations, corpus replay and evidence freshness |
| Release candidate | Frozen integrated revision, applicable #2623/#2958/#2940 obligations and actual production package consumption |

Reuse and improve existing tiers. Do not add a full multi-day Cartesian campaign to every PR. Test the shipped package/configuration for release sign-off, not only a test-instrumented assembly from a nearby commit.

---

# 7. Run a bounded independent integrated audit

Initial cadence proposal: weekly during active storage/concurrency development, after related protocol merges, and before release qualification. Define the responsible maintainer/rotation and where the report is stored; do not leave ownership and cadence unspecified indefinitely.

Each audit freezes a revision and starts from the contracts and supported state inventory, not from an author's explanation of why their patch is safe. Then review changes since the last validated revision, including tests and CI.

Prioritize:

- persistent states and transitions absent from the fault model;
- interactions without an executed lifecycle scenario;
- historical states whose expected outcome changed;
- silent wrong results, stale recovery selection or mixed generations;
- snapshot/ownership/cleanup and retry paths;
- weakened tests, new skips, broad expected-error allowances, repinned corpora and missing/stale evidence;
- divergence between current implementation, shipped behavior and rule documents.

Produce a compact report:

```
revision + baseline
contracts/scenarios/fault models checked
observed coverage and artifact/replay references
findings + classification + severity + owner
blocked decisions and explicit untested scope
next targeted investigation or accepted follow-up
```

A single maintainer can operate this process. A separate adversarial review pass and independently designed oracle are useful; requiring two available human maintainers is not a prerequisite. An LLM review can propose counterexamples, but agreement between agents is not experimental evidence or merge approval.

## Classify findings and act on them

Distinguish **introduced regression**, **pre-existing defect newly exposed**, **harness/CI defect**, **documented semantic difference**, and **unknown origin**. Record failing/fixed revisions and causal evidence when available. More bugs discovered after a merge does not by itself establish that the merge introduced them.

Confirmed product failures become focused tests and permanent corpus cases where useful. Fix the concrete defect; revise a general rule only when there is a reusable lesson. Keep harness changes and independent product fixes separately reviewable where practical.

For a new unexplained safety failure, pause further merges touching the implicated protocol until it is classified and the relevant gate is restored. A known data-loss or silent-result defect in supported release behavior is not resolved by documenting it or adding retries. Use #2623 for the release disposition.

Any legitimate quarantine needs an owner, reason, expiry/review point and visible coverage gap. It cannot count as passing evidence for the affected safety contract. Unrelated old failures must be tracked honestly rather than making every small PR an unbounded whole-engine repair task.

## Define when review is finished

Before a high-risk merge/campaign, agree on a finite gate: affected contracts, selected scenario/fault matrix, required platforms, semantic coverage assertions and bounded run budget.

The gate is complete when that evidence passes on the accepted candidate, failures are classified, and no unresolved blocker remains in scope. New concrete counterexamples reopen the affected gate; speculative unrelated improvements become follow-ups.

“No bug found in this campaign” is bounded evidence, not proof of universal safety. Conversely, “we could always run more tests” must not make completion impossible.

---

# 8. Preserve history as narrow, revision-specific examples

Use “failure that motivated the rule” and “good pattern,” not “bad PR” and “good PR.” Keep the normative rule concise, add at most 1–2 examples beside it, and link exact commits/tests where practical. A useful example is not an endorsement of every claim in a large historical PR description.

| Lesson | Failure / motivation | Good pattern and limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model complete recovery states, not independent rollback branches | #2972 → #2977/#2979: mismatched data/WAL or a valid-looking stale original | #2978 (`a809c7d95eceaa7b2e7d2c0dec6fe7557d25723d`): `Rebuild_InstallFaultMatrix_Tests`, original pair / complete replacement / guarded incomplete state; guard against missing new registered failure points |
| Audit the fault model itself | #3011: rebuild rename/marker directory-persistence concerns | Complement #2978's install/rollback model with actual namespace-persistence boundaries; do not present the existing matrix as complete hardware power-loss proof |
| A test must prove its named transition | #3026 / #3031: four inserts could follow a single handoff | #3033, [pinned test source](https://github.com/litedb-org/LiteDB/blob/d2a1d9d0dd726c5f3342fb19e0b641d3b6137be3/LiteDB.Tests/Engine/SharedReaderPin_Tests.cs): ready → fresh owner update/re-pin → release → completion for each attempt; separate tight-loop coverage remains |
| Use real producer binaries and interrupted historical states | #2998: a released engine could append after interrupted checksum conversion | Released 5.0.21 and actual-v9 validation, full payload/index models and old-engine rejection; these are historical layer-specific outcomes, not blanket current support for every legacy read-only path |
| Preserve supported degraded behavior without weakening guarantees | #2998 / #2242: unsupported sync versus actual I/O failure | Explicit operation-specific durability/fallback contracts and diagnostics; do not generalize one historical fallback decision to every later publication/reclamation protocol |
| Cleanup and owner death are data-integrity operations | #3005: disposing an orphaned engine could checkpoint stale state | #3003 commit `8fdce766f`: discard without checkpoint; PR-reported held-reader evidence was 100/100 losses before and 200/200 passes after, not a universal statistical guarantee |
| Coordination ABI and fallback are part of compatibility | #3016's prototype/authority evolution | Version/capability/layout/identity checks, unknown-authority preservation, explicit qualified fast path and fallback; test supported mixed participants and refusal separately |

#2998's validation and #3016's reports also demonstrate why evidence must identify the revision: measurements and claims from earlier heads must not silently become claims about a later integrated tree.

---

# 9. Implementation order and finite acceptance

## Phase A — adopt the process using current tooling

- [ ] Add the five-prompt PR section and link existing rule documents.
- [ ] Document risk selection, test-replacement accounting, precise failure/outcome contracts, ownership and bounded completion criteria.
- [ ] Establish a small invariant-to-evidence index by extending the existing audit/report structure; avoid another specification.
- [ ] Inventory existing suites/fixtures against the first selected contracts and explicitly record gaps.
- [ ] Add a **coverage-regression inventory/check** for removed test methods/files, new or broadened skips, narrowed CI filters/partitions, changed timeouts, expected-error allowlists, fixture generators and corpus repins. Conditional tests such as platform/capability facts must be shown to execute on at least one intended CI leg. Changes need an explicit invariant/coverage disposition rather than silently becoming less coverage.
- [ ] Establish a **persistent-boundary / crash-point registry**: enumerate registered crash/fault points and map each to the test/fuzz scenario that claims it. Separately audit the actual I/O/rename/publication/ownership sequence so transitions with no registered hook can be discovered; 100% registered-hook coverage is not treated as proof that the fault model is complete.
- [ ] Decide and document the compatibility policy for **publicly published prerelease packages/formats**. At minimum, files written by an in-scope published prerelease must either be read/migrated according to the declared contract or rejected without mutation; they must never be silently misinterpreted. Define the bounded retained package/version window separately rather than accidentally promising support for every historical prerelease forever.
- [ ] Publish one baseline integrated audit report tied to an exact revision, without marking unrun checks as passed.

## Phase B — enforce evidence and prove it works

- [ ] Implement/extend the stable aggregate evidence check; verify real applicability, discovery, runtime/hook selection, revision and missing/skipped/canceled-result behavior.
- [ ] Enforce the coverage-regression check in CI with a reviewed baseline/exception ledger so pre-existing skips are not mistaken for new regressions.
- [ ] Make the persistent-boundary registry executable: adding/removing a registered crash point must update its claimed evidence, while protocol audits can report an explicit uncovered transition even when no hook exists yet.
- [ ] Define and enforce candidate-tree validation through a tested merge-queue or serialized-merge procedure. Repository-settings changes are a separate explicit implementation action.
- [ ] Pilot the process on existing mechanisms: rebuild/recovery pairing, repeated snapshot/reclamation/owner turnover, and real historical upgrade followed by indexed mutations and cold reopen.
- [ ] Demonstrate an existing unsafe state or deliberately broken variant is caught, an unexecuted required path fails the gate, and a legitimate non-applicable case does not trigger unnecessary campaigns.
- [ ] Add manifest/provenance/outcome information to representative existing compatibility fixtures, preserving originals and their logical oracles.
- [ ] Exercise the selected published-prerelease compatibility policy against a bounded set of actual packages/produced files, including at least safe read/migrate/reject behavior and source-byte preservation where rejection is expected.

## Phase C — operate and refine

- [ ] Reuse scheduled full CI/fuzz runs for revision-aware integrated evidence and triaged failure reporting.
- [ ] Run the first independent bounded refinement session, link findings/dispositions and identify the next owner/cadence.
- [ ] Feed confirmed escapes into focused regressions/corpora; update general rules only for reusable lessons.
- [ ] Track a few useful signals: unresolved safety findings, required scenarios lacking fresh evidence, unexplained skips/retries, and whether known bad variants are detected. Do not optimize raw test counts or treat fewer discovered bugs as proof of quality.

**This issue is complete when the process is documented, enforced for its selected obligations, demonstrated on the pilots, and has an operating owner/reporting path.** Future audits and expansion of the corpus continue afterward. Full formal verification, every historical binary, every platform/fault combination, a new public integrity API, and a new fuzzing framework are not implicit prerequisites.

Concrete product defects discovered during implementation remain separately tracked and are not closed merely because this process issue is complete.

## External rationale (supporting references, not a replacement specification)

- [SQLite testing](https://www.sqlite.org/testing.html): independent harnesses, I/O/crash and compound-failure testing, regression corpora and mutation testing provide complementary evidence.
- [GitHub merge-queue documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue) and [required-check troubleshooting](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud%40latest/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks): candidate integration checks and explicit handling of skipped/missing checks.
- [Linux `fsync(2)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html): syncing file content does not necessarily persist its containing directory entry; fault models must include the filesystem operations the protocol actually relies on.
title: Make PR safety review and integrated regression audits explicit
